hops.title: Adult canaries hinted that radial cells make neurons
hops.text: Adult canaries keep making new projection neurons for the song-control pathway, and the new cells replace older ones; species and seasonal comparisons suggested a link to learning. In 1990 Arturo Alvarez-Buylla, Marga Theelen and Fernando Nottebohm mapped tritiated-thymidine-labeled cells in the walls of the adult canary's lateral ventricles. The labeled cells bunched into hot spots that matched regions rich in radial cells and the sites where new neurons originate. Smears from those hot spots showed the radial cells themselves taking up the label and dividing. The authors suggested that radial cells give rise to the new neurons, about ten years before the rodent work above.

image.caption: Dividing radial cells in adult canary brains pointed to a source of new neurons a decade before rodent proof.

hops.title: A human gene folds a marmoset's smooth cortex
hops.text: Common marmosets are small monkeys with a naturally smooth cortex. Humans carry a gene no other living primate has, ARHGAP11B, which began as a partial copy of an older gene, ARHGAP11A. A single C-to-G change in the copy created a new splice site, so 55 nucleotides drop out of the mRNA, the reading frame shifts, and the protein ends in a new tail. In 2020 Michael Heide, Wieland Huttner and colleagues studied fetal marmosets expressing the human gene under its own human promoter. Outer (basal) radial glia increased in the outer subventricular zone, upper-layer neurons increased, and the cortex grew larger and folded.

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A small common marmoset with white ear tufts perched curiously on a mossy branch.
image.caption: A human-specific gene added outer radial glia in fetal marmosets, and their smooth cortex grew and folded.

hops.title: Rhesus cortical progenitors divide more slowly than a mouse's
hops.text: A rhesus monkey's neocortex is about 100 times larger than a mouse's, so a reasonable guess is that its progenitors divide faster. In 1998 David Kornack and Pasko Rakic timed ventricular-zone progenitors in fetal rhesus monkeys and found the reverse. Against the mouse's 8 to 18 hours, the monkey cycle took about 23 hours at embryonic day 40 and about 54 hours at day 60, up to five times longer. The monkey wins on time instead. Its cortical neurogenesis lasts about 60 days against the mouse's 6. By the authors' estimate, days 40 to 80 alone fit about 28 rounds of division; the whole mouse window fits about 11.

sources.citation: Kornack & Rakic, Proc. Natl. Acad. Sci. U.S.A. 95:1242-1246 (1998)

image.caption: Rhesus progenitors divide more slowly than mouse progenitors but keep neurogenesis running ten times longer.

audio.title: Canaries, marmosets and a slow monkey clock
audio.transcript:
For a long time, radial glia were described as scaffolding: long fibres that young neurons climb on their way out to the cortex. Here are three stories about how much more they do, and about the experiments that made the case.

The first comes from birds. Around nineteen ninety, Fernando Nottebohm's group at Rockefeller University reported that adult canaries keep making new projection neurons in the pathway that controls song, and that the new neurons replace older ones. The group's comparisons across species and seasons suggested that this turnover might be linked to learning. That left an obvious question. Where were the new neurons coming from? Arturo Alvarez-Buylla, Marga Theelen and Nottebohm used tritiated thymidine, which marks cells copying their D N A, and mapped where labeled cells appeared in the walls of the adult canary's lateral ventricles. The labeled cells were not spread evenly. They bunched into hot spots, and the hot spots lined up with regions rich in radial cells and with the places where new neurons start. To check, the team made smears from small fragments of those hot spots and found that the radial cells themselves had taken up the label and were dividing. They suggested, carefully, that radial cell division might give rise to new neurons. That was about ten years before experiments in mice and rats showed that, in the embryonic cortex, the scaffold is also the source.

The second story is about one human gene. Humans carry a gene called A R H G A P eleven B. It began as a partial copy of an older gene, A R H G A P eleven A, which other primates have too. Then a single letter in the copy changed, a C to a G. That one change created a new splice site, so fifty-five nucleotides are cut out of the gene's messenger R N A, the reading frame shifts, and the protein ends in a new tail. Modern humans carry that change, and so did Neanderthals and Denisovans. No other living primate has the gene at all. In twenty twenty, Michael Heide, Wieland Huttner and colleagues in Germany and Japan studied fetal common marmosets that expressed the human gene, switched on by its own human promoter. Marmosets are small monkeys with a smooth cortex. In the fetuses carrying the human gene, basal radial glia increased in the outer subventricular zone, upper-layer neurons increased, the neocortex grew larger, and its smooth surface folded. One human gene added basal radial glia and produced changes like those seen in human cortical development.

The third story starts with a reasonable guess that turned out wrong. A rhesus monkey's neocortex is about a hundred times larger than a mouse's, so you might expect its progenitors to divide faster. In nineteen ninety-eight, David Kornack and Pasko Rakic timed ventricular-zone progenitors in fetal rhesus monkeys. A mouse progenitor finishes a cycle in about eight to eighteen hours. The monkey cycle took about twenty-three hours at embryonic day forty and stretched to about fifty-four hours by day sixty, up to five times longer. The monkey makes up for it with time. Its cortical neurogenesis runs about sixty days, against six in the mouse. Kornack and Rakic estimated about twenty-eight rounds of division between embryonic days forty and eighty alone. The entire mouse window fits about eleven. The rhesus monkey does not run the factory faster. It keeps it open longer.
